request.job_description: We are hiring a Frontend Engineer to build and maintain accessible, high-quality product UI in React and TypeScript. You will own features end to end, collaborate with design and backend engineers, contribute to a shared component library, and help raise the bar on accessibility, performance, and testing. Experience meeting WCAG 2.1 AA, profiling rendering performance, and writing maintainable typed code is expected.

transcript.question: Tell me about a time you made a complex UI component accessible. What was the component and how did you approach it?
transcript.answer: We had a custom combobox in our design system that was used in about 40 screens and failed screen reader testing. I audited it against the WAI-ARIA authoring practices combobox pattern, and found three problems: focus was moving into the listbox instead of staying on the input, aria-activedescendant wasn't being updated, and the selected option wasn't announced. I rewrote it to keep DOM focus on the input and manage aria-activedescendant, added live region announcements for result counts, and handled Escape and Home/End keys. I tested with NVDA on Windows and VoiceOver on Mac, and added axe checks in CI. The trade-off was a breaking API change to the onChange signature, so I shipped a codemod and a deprecation window of one release. Afterward our external audit dropped from 14 issues on that flow to 2.

transcript.question: How do you use TypeScript to make a shared component library safer for other engineers to use?
transcript.answer: I lean on discriminated unions for props that are mutually exclusive. For example, our Button took either a label or an icon-only mode, and icon-only requires aria-label. I typed it so that if iconOnly is true, aria-label is required, so the compiler catches the accessibility mistake. I also use generics for our Select so the value type flows through onChange, and I avoid enums in favor of const objects with as const. One trade-off is that heavy conditional types hurt error message readability, so I keep them to the public API and add doc comments with examples. We also run tsc with strict and noUncheckedIndexedAccess.

transcript.question: Describe a performance problem you debugged in a React app.
transcript.answer: We had a data table with around 2,000 rows that took roughly 900ms to respond to a filter keystroke. I used the React Profiler and saw that every row re-rendered because a parent created a new callback and a new options object each render. I memoized the row with React.memo, stabilized the callbacks with useCallback, and moved the derived filtering into useMemo. That dropped it to about 120ms, but it was still not great, so I added windowing with react-window, which got it under 30ms. The windowing broke find-in-page and screen reader row counts, so I added aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex to keep it accessible. I verified results with a Lighthouse trace and recorded before and after numbers in the PR.

transcript.question: What is your approach to testing UI code, and where do you draw the line?
transcript.answer: I use React Testing Library and query by role and accessible name, which gives accessibility coverage for free, because if getByRole fails, a screen reader user likely has a problem too. I keep unit tests for logic like reducers and formatters, integration tests for flows with mock service worker, and a small number of Playwright end-to-end tests for critical paths like checkout. I avoid snapshot tests for big trees because they get rubber-stamped. On my last team, we got flaky e2e tests down from about 8% to under 1% by removing fixed sleeps and waiting on network idle and specific UI states.

transcript.question: Tell me about a disagreement with a designer or another engineer and how you handled it.
transcript.answer: A designer wanted a custom dropdown with hover-only menus and low-contrast placeholder text for visual polish. I didn't just say no. I measured the contrast at 2.8:1 against the 4.5:1 requirement and demoed the hover menu with keyboard only to show it was unreachable. Then I proposed two alternatives and prototyped one in Storybook within a day. We agreed on a click-activated menu with a slightly darker placeholder, and the designer later added contrast checks to their Figma workflow. I owned the follow-up by writing a short accessibility guideline page for the design system.
